subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT usually a government economic objective?
options: Low inflation
Low unemployment
Economic growth
Maximising the profit of private firms
questions.explain: Governments aim for low inflation, low unemployment, economic growth and a balance of payments equilibrium, not to maximise private firms' profits.

questions.q: Inflation is best defined as:
options: A general and sustained rise in the average level of prices
A rise in the total output of an economy
A fall in the number of people out of work
An increase in a country's exports
questions.explain: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money.

questions.q: A period of falling Gross Domestic Product (negative economic growth) is known as a:
options: Recession
Boom
Surplus
Subsidy
questions.explain: A recession is a period during which national output (GDP) falls, typically raising unemployment and reducing demand.

questions.q: What is the most likely effect on businesses when the central bank raises interest rates?
options: Borrowing becomes more expensive, so investment and consumer spending tend to fall
Consumer spending rises sharply as saving becomes less attractive
Exports automatically become cheaper for foreign buyers
Inflation immediately rises because prices go up
questions.explain: Higher interest rates raise the cost of loans, discouraging borrowing, investment and spending on credit.

questions.q: An increase in the rate of income tax is most likely to:
options: Reduce consumers' disposable income and lower demand for goods
Increase consumers' disposable income and raise demand
Have no effect on how much households can spend
Automatically reduce a firm's production costs
questions.explain: Higher income tax leaves households with less disposable income, reducing spending on many products.

questions.q: Unemployment refers to people who are:
options: Willing and able to work but cannot find a job
Choosing to retire early
Working part-time by choice
Studying full-time at school or college
questions.explain: The unemployed are those able and actively seeking work but without a job.

questions.q: During a period of economic growth, a business selling consumer goods is most likely to experience:
options: Higher demand as consumers have more income to spend
Lower demand because prices always fall
No change in sales at all
An automatic fall in its costs of production
questions.explain: Economic growth raises incomes and employment, generally increasing consumer demand for goods and services.

questions.q: A furniture retailer relies on customers taking out loans to buy expensive sofas. Interest rates have just risen sharply. What is the likely impact on the retailer?
options: Sales are likely to fall as loans cost customers more
Sales are likely to rise as loans become cheaper
Its supply costs will automatically fall
Its exports will immediately increase
questions.explain: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer, so demand for credit-financed big-ticket items tends to fall.

questions.q: A multinational company (MNC) is best described as a business that:
options: Has operations or production based in more than one country
Sells only to customers within its home country
Is owned entirely by a national government
Employs fewer than ten workers
questions.explain: An MNC has production or operations located in more than one country.

questions.q: Imports are:
options: Goods and services bought from other countries
Goods and services sold to other countries
Taxes placed on foreign goods
Limits on the quantity of foreign goods allowed in
questions.explain: Imports are goods and services purchased from abroad; exports are those sold abroad.

questions.q: A tariff is:
options: A tax placed on imported goods
A physical limit on the quantity of imports
A payment made by government to help exporters
A ban on trade with a particular country
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price to protect domestic producers.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes globalisation?
options: The growing integration and interdependence of the world's economies
The process of a firm selling only in its home market
A government limiting trade with other nations
The closing down of multinational companies
questions.explain: Globalisation is the increasing connection and interdependence of economies through trade and investment.

questions.q: One benefit of a multinational company setting up in a host (developing) country is that it can:
options: Create jobs and bring new skills and technology
Guarantee that all profits stay in the host country
Remove all competition for local firms permanently
Eliminate the need for any government taxation
questions.explain: MNCs can provide employment, training, investment and technology transfer in the host country.

questions.q: A common drawback of multinational companies for a host country is that:
options: Profits may be sent back to the home country rather than reinvested locally
They always pay lower wages than the law allows
They never employ any local workers
They are always owned by the host government
questions.explain: MNCs may repatriate profits to their home country and can out-compete smaller local firms.

questions.q: If a country's currency appreciates (becomes stronger), the most likely effect is that:
options: Exports become dearer abroad and imports become cheaper
Exports become cheaper abroad and imports become dearer
Both exports and imports become cheaper
Neither exports nor imports are affected
questions.explain: A stronger currency raises export prices in foreign markets and lowers the price of imports (SPICED).

questions.q: A UK clothing manufacturer sells most of its output to customers in Europe. The pound suddenly rises strongly against the euro. What is the likely effect on the firm?
options: Its goods become more expensive for European buyers, so export sales may fall
Its goods become cheaper for European buyers, so export sales will rise
The cost of its imported raw materials will rise
Its European sales will be completely unaffected
questions.explain: A stronger pound raises the euro price of the firm's exports, likely reducing demand abroad.

questions.q: A business imports most of its raw materials from abroad. Its home currency has just depreciated (weakened). What is the likely impact?
options: Its import costs rise, increasing its costs of production
Its import costs fall, reducing its costs of production
Its export prices rise for foreign buyers
Its costs are unaffected by the exchange rate
questions.explain: A weaker currency makes imports more expensive, raising the cost of imported raw materials.

questions.q: An external cost (negative externality) of business activity is best illustrated by:
options: Pollution from a factory that harms the local community
Wages paid to a firm's own workers
Rent paid by a business for its premises
Interest a firm pays on a bank loan
questions.explain: External costs are costs of production paid by third parties or society, such as pollution, not by the firm itself.

questions.q: Sustainable development means meeting present needs:
options: Without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs
By using up natural resources as quickly as possible
By always choosing the cheapest production method
Only if it increases short-term profit
questions.explain: Sustainability involves using resources so that future generations can still meet their own needs.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a business acting ethically?
options: Refusing to use child labour even though it would cut costs
Dumping waste in a river to save money
Misleading customers in its advertising
Paying suppliers less than the agreed price
questions.explain: Ethical behaviour means doing what is morally right, such as avoiding child labour, even if it lowers profit.

questions.q: Why might behaving ethically create a conflict for a business?
options: Ethical decisions can raise costs and reduce short-term profit
Ethical decisions always lower a firm's costs
Ethical behaviour is required to break the law
Customers never care about ethical behaviour
questions.explain: Ethical choices such as fair wages or cleaner production often increase costs, conflicting with short-term profit.

questions.q: A coffee company decides to pay farmers a guaranteed fair price and use recyclable packaging. The most likely combined effect is:
options: Higher production costs but an improved brand image that may attract customers
Lower costs and a worse reputation
No change to costs or reputation
Immediate elimination of all competitors
questions.explain: Ethical and environmental measures usually raise costs but can strengthen brand image and customer loyalty.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Business Studies (0450) syllabus; External Influences on Business Activity
